title: Koala fingerprints can be mistaken for human ones
body: Koalas have loops, whorls and arches on their fingertips so similar to ours that even under a microscope they are hard to tell apart. Koalas and humans last shared an ancestor over 100 million years ago, so the feature evolved separately in each.
takeaway: When unrelated animals face the same problem, here gripping and feeling, evolution often lands on the same answer.
visual: a koala's paw gripping a eucalyptus branch in close view, the fine ridges on its fingertips catching the light

title: Checkmate comes from the Persian for the king is helpless
body: Chess began in India around the sixth century as chaturanga, a game of four army divisions: infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots. It passed to Persia, where the words shah mat announced a trapped king, and then through the Arab world to Europe.
takeaway: The bishop was originally an elephant and the rook a chariot. The queen became the strongest piece only around 1500.
source: H. J. R. Murray, A History of Chess (1913)
visual: an ancient carved game board with pieces shaped as elephants, chariots, horses and foot soldiers, lit by an oil lamp

title: The world's shortest scheduled flight lasts about 90 seconds
body: Loganair flies between the Scottish islands of Westray and Papa Westray, 2.7 km apart. The timetable allows two minutes, and with a tailwind the hop has been done in 53 seconds. The distance is shorter than the runway at many large airports.
takeaway: It is a lifeline, not a stunt. Teachers, patients and schoolchildren depend on it.
visual: a tiny propeller plane crossing a narrow strip of grey sea between two low green islands

title: There is no Nobel Prize in mathematics
body: Alfred Nobel's will named physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace. Nobody knows for certain why he left maths out, and the popular story about a romantic rival has no evidence behind it. Mathematicians have the Fields Medal and the Abel Prize.
takeaway: The economics prize is not an original Nobel either. Sweden's central bank created it in 1968.
source: Nobel Prize Organisation; International Mathematical Union
visual: a row of five gleaming gold medals on dark velvet with one empty space at the end

title: The Statue of Liberty used to be brown
body: The statue's skin is copper, about 2.4 mm thick, and it was the colour of a new coin when it was unveiled in 1886. Air and rain slowly turned it green, and by about 1920 the change was complete. The green layer protects the metal beneath.
takeaway: In 1906 officials planned to repaint it. The public objected, and engineers found the green coat was doing useful work.
visual: a colossal torch-bearing statue shown half in gleaming copper brown and half in weathered green against a harbour sky

title: Ketchup began as a fish sauce
body: The word comes from ke-tsiap, a fermented fish sauce from the coast of southern China. British traders brought the idea home around 1700 and made versions from mushrooms, walnuts and oysters. Tomatoes first appear in an American recipe of 1812.
takeaway: Recipes travel and change much faster than their names do.
source: Dan Jurafsky, The Language of Food (2014)
visual: clay jars of dark sauce on the deck of an old sailing ship in a southern Chinese harbour, a few ripe tomatoes beside them

title: Tug of war and poetry were once Olympic events
body: Tug of war was contested at five Olympic Games between 1900 and 1920. From 1912 to 1948 the Olympics also gave medals for architecture, literature, music, painting and sculpture, provided the work was inspired by sport.
takeaway: Pierre de Coubertin, founder of the modern Games, won the 1912 gold medal for literature under a false name.
visual: two early 1900s teams in long shorts straining at a thick rope on a grass field, a sculptor working at an easel nearby

title: British stamps are the only ones without a country's name
body: Britain issued the world's first adhesive postage stamp, the Penny Black, in 1840. Since no other stamps existed, there was no need to say where it came from. By international agreement Britain still shows only the monarch's head.
takeaway: Before stamps, the person receiving a letter usually paid for it, and many refused.
visual: a small black Victorian postage stamp with a queen's profile on an old handwritten envelope sealed with red wax

title: One country has about 840 living languages
body: Papua New Guinea has roughly 10 million people and around 840 languages, more than any other country and about 12% of all the languages on Earth. Steep mountains, dense forest and swamps kept communities apart for thousands of years.
takeaway: India is fourth with about 450. Around 40% of the world's languages are now at risk of dying out.
visual: a mountainous tropical island with dozens of separate villages in deep valleys, each sending up its own thread of smoke

title: The world's biggest tyre maker is a toy company
body: Counted by number, LEGO produces more tyres than any other company: over 300 million a year, all of them tiny. Guinness World Records confirmed the title in 2011. The company made its first rubber tyre in 1962.
takeaway: How you count decides who wins. By weight or value, LEGO is nowhere near the top.
visual: a mountain of tiny black toy tyres pouring from a factory chute, one full-size car tyre standing beside it for scale
